opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, partly because I've lived on both sides: most of my career in academia, some time in industry, and now building a company.

I'd say the ecosystem is incredibly vibrant, but it's becoming lopsided, and that worries me. The energy, talent, and capital flowing into commercial labs is extraordinary, and a lot of good comes from it. These labs are shipping technology that real people use, and they're pushing the frontier in ways that would have been hard to imagine even five years ago.

But a healthy ecosystem isn't a monoculture. When I look at universities and public-sector research right now, there's a real resource gap. Many academic labs can't train or even meaningfully study frontier-scale models. Graduate students who want to work on the most important questions sometimes feel they have to leave for industry just to get access to compute and data. When that happens, we lose something important, because academia has a distinct role. It does curiosity-driven, long-horizon research that doesn't have to justify itself on a product roadmap. It does independent evaluation and auditing. It studies the societal implications of the technology. And it trains the next generation, not just of engineers but of thinkers.

That's why I've spent a lot of time advocating for public investment in AI infrastructure, things like a national research cloud that gives researchers in universities and the public sector shared access to compute and data. It isn't about competing with industry. It's about making sure the people asking the foundational questions, and the people holding the technology accountable, aren't locked out.

The other dimension of health I care about is who gets to participate. If AI is going to shape every part of human life, the people building it and studying it need to reflect humanity: different disciplines, different backgrounds, different perspectives. That's a big part of why human-centered AI matters to me. The technology is ultimately about people, so the ecosystem that builds it has to include more than a handful of companies.

So I'm optimistic, genuinely. But optimism isn't the same as complacency. We have to be deliberate about rebalancing, so that the open science, the public interest research, and the diversity of ideas that got us here in the first place stay strong.

r001.rationale: The response centers its concern on academia’s resource gap and researchers being locked out, while describing commercial labs’ growth positively and saying the issue is not competing with industry.

r002.rationale: It calls industry’s shipping of technology used by real people a good contribution to the ecosystem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it as a question of balance, and right now the balance is off.

When I started in this field, the big ideas came from universities. ImageNet came out of academia. Backpropagation, convolutional networks, the foundations of deep learning all came from a research ecosystem that was broadly distributed and publicly funded. Today the frontier has moved almost entirely into a handful of commercial labs, and that shift has happened faster than most of us expected.

I want to be fair to the companies. The scale of compute and engineering required to train today's models is genuinely enormous, and private capital has delivered breakthroughs that would not have happened otherwise. I don't think the answer is to resent that or wish it away.

But a healthy ecosystem needs more than one kind of player. Universities do things that companies structurally cannot. They work on problems with no obvious product. They train the next generation, which is the real pipeline for the whole field. They publish openly and take risks on ideas that might take fifteen years to pay off. And they can ask the questions that are uncomfortable for a company to ask about its own technology.

What worries me is that academic labs today often cannot access the compute or the data to even participate in frontier research. A graduate student at a top university may have fewer resources than an intern at a large lab. That is not a sustainable situation. It means we are concentrating not just capability but also the ability to study and evaluate these systems in very few hands.

This is why I have spent a lot of my time on the policy side, pushing for public investment in compute and data, for a national research resource, so that universities and nonprofits can stay in the game. I think of it as the public sector doing what it has always done well, which is funding the long-term, open, foundational science.

The other thing I would say is that talent flow matters. Many of us have moved between academia and industry, and that can be very healthy. It becomes unhealthy when the flow is only one direction, when every strong student leaves and no one comes back. I have tried in my own career to keep a foot in both worlds because I believe each one needs the other.

So my honest assessment is that the ecosystem is vibrant in terms of pace and excitement, but fragile in terms of diversity. Diversity of institutions, of incentives, of people, and of the questions being asked. If we lose that, I think we eventually lose the engine that made the current moment possible in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says its main worry is that academic labs lack the compute and data to participate, while describing commercial labs’ growth as understandable and not something to resent or wish away.

r002.rationale: It credits private capital with enabling breakthroughs and describes the ecosystem’s pace as exciting, but does not clearly characterize rapid industry AI product development as a positive contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think a healthy AI ecosystem needs both strong industry research and strong public research. Industry brings extraordinary resources and the ability to turn discoveries into products. That’s valuable. But universities have a different role: they train the next generation, pursue questions whose payoff may be many years away, and create space for work that doesn’t have an immediate commercial incentive.

My concern is the growing gap in access to compute, data, and talent. If only a handful of companies can pursue certain kinds of research, that narrows who gets to ask the questions—and ultimately, whose needs the technology serves.

So we need to invest in public research infrastructure and support academic researchers. We also need room for disciplines beyond computer science, because understanding AI’s effects requires expertise in everything from medicine to the social sciences. The health of the ecosystem isn’t just about how fast we advance the technology. It’s about whether we sustain the breadth of people and ideas needed to make that progress beneficial.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the growing gap in access to compute, data, and talent as a concern, but it does not compare that concern with pressure from commercial AI labs or say it is greater.

r002.rationale: The response says industry can turn discoveries into products and explicitly calls that valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the growth of commercial labs brings tremendous energy and resources, and that can accelerate discovery. But the health of the research ecosystem depends on more than what happens inside a handful of companies.

Universities have a very important role: educating the next generation, asking questions that may not have an immediate commercial return, and making knowledge available to the public. If researchers and students cannot access the compute and data they need to participate, we risk narrowing both who can contribute and which questions get asked.

So I would look at this as a question of balance. We need strong industry research, strong public investment, and a vibrant academic community. And we need pathways for collaboration that preserve researchers’ independence. AI will affect all of society; the opportunity to shape it should be broadly shared.

r001.rationale: The response notes that limited academic access to compute and data can narrow participation, but it does not express greater concern about academia’s resource disadvantage than about pressure from commercial labs.

r002.rationale: It describes commercial labs’ growth and resources as accelerating discovery, but does not characterize rapid industry product development as a positive contribution.
